definition.text: The history of economic thought is the study of the thinkers and theories behind political economy and economics, from the ancient world to today.

facts.text: In the West, economics was part of philosophy rather than a separate discipline until the Industrial Revolution of the 18th and 19th centuries.
Mercantilism dominated Europe from the 16th to the 18th century, until the physiocrats and then Adam Smith's classical economics challenged it.
Neoclassical economics developed in the 1870s in three independent schools: the Cambridge, Austrian and Lausanne schools.
In 1920 Arthur Cecil Pigou argued that markets fail when there are externalities, so the state must step in.
In the 1930s economists began modelling how to manage non-renewable resources and whether welfare can be sustained in an economy that uses them up.
Malthus on overpopulation and Mill on the stationary state anticipated the concerns of ecological economics, founded in the work of Boulding, Georgescu-Roegen and Daly.

title: Mercantilism

definition.text: Mercantilism is a nationalist economic policy that aims to maximize a country's exports and minimize its imports.

facts.text: Mercantilists held that money and precious metals were the only true riches, so tariffs should encourage exports and discourage imports.
They believed international trade could not benefit all countries at once.
It dominated modernizing Europe from the 16th to the 19th centuries; Adam Smith vigorously opposed it and argued for free trade.

title: Neoclassical economics

definition.text: Neoclassical economics is the approach that explains production, consumption and prices through supply and demand.

facts.text: In this view a good's value comes from individuals maximizing their satisfaction within their incomes and firms maximizing profit given their costs.
It developed in the 1870s and replaced classical economics as the mainstream, also in the English-speaking world.
Its Lausanne School, led by Léon Walras and Vilfredo Pareto, developed general equilibrium and Pareto efficiency.
It is the dominant approach to microeconomics today.
